speechtext:
-the proposed changes included a reduction of premiums. I believe this minister may have obtained some of his skill in numbers from the former minister who proposed the changes in 1971. That minister was confident that he was
November 9, 1978

going to save money through the changes although the premiums were actually being reduced. It was the old Liberal trick again-they indicated they had discovered how to pay out more benefits at less cost. I have a chart here, Mr. Speaker, which will show how they worked it out.
It became obvious that the combined premiums of employer and employee could never meet the cost of the program. With the abolition of the unemployment insurance fund, general revenue moneys were transferred to the unemployment insurance account without the requirement of a vote in this House. That is where the present minister comes in with his cute terminology. We are straightforward people on this side of the House and it seems to us that if you spend $4 billion when you only have an income of $2 billion, you end up with a deficit of $2 billion. The minister refers to it as a "commitment" and apparently believes the taxpayer is willing to make up the shortfall.
It is interesting to know that these tricks used by the government result, as the Auditor General noted recently, in an overstatement of the assets on the statement of assets and liabilities of Canada of some $2 billion because the expenditures are not matched with the fiscal period into which they should fall. For instance, on March 31, 1978, the statement of assets and liabilities of Canada shows a 12 billion advance to the unemployment insurance account. It will never be recovered, yet it is shown as an asset. It will be written off next year. Not all of us can defer a $2 billion expenditure into another accounting period.
Since 1971, despite the increase in premiums, combined payments have never covered the cost of the program. The schedule I have here shows that in 1970-71, the year before most Liberal amendments were made, the deficit or shortfall or whatever was $300 million. Immediately after the changes were made in 1971, the deficit was $686 million. It ranged around the billion dollar mark in 1975, last year it was $1.6 billion, and although the figures for 1978 are not final, the interim figures are sufficient to show that the deficit will be over $2 billion this year.
That is not the only problem, Mr. Speaker. An additional problem is the precipitous increase in labour turnovers. The costs of those turnovers may represent our single largest factor in terms of lost productivity. It is very difficult to quantify that kind of a figure but it could well exceed the losses in Canada due to strikes. Concerning the strike situation in Canada we find that the Prime Minister said that Canada has the worst record for strikes.
Again, that is not the only problem members have had. Members on all sides of the House have found themselves over the past six or seven years turned into ombudsmen for unemployment insurance claims. The jungle of the Unemployment Insurance Commission has become vast and I have forgotten how many of hundreds of offices there are. The number of unemployed is so great that Canadians cannot cope with the system themselves and the number of appeals to members of
Unemployment Insurance
parliament has become enormous. Largely these problems are caused by inequities in the system as it now exists. We were quite hopeful the minister would give us some kind of a program that would clear up these inequities. I would like to mention a few, especially the forcing, through the regulations, of self-employed and retired taxpayers to contribute to the deficit through the income tax system. That may not seem unusual, but if we are going to have an insurance scheme, and the government still persists in calling it an unemployment insurance scheme, then to force individuals to pay for that scheme without permitting them to participate in the benefits, because they have no coverage, certainly has to be considered inequitable.
According to the annual report of the unemployment insurance account, which I have here, the total cost to the government for the extended benefit period of the program-and the minister indicates that is all paid by the government-is over $1 billion. The total cost to the government in the 1977 calendar year was approaching $2 billion. The interesting factor that is revealed by the financial statements, however, is for phase 2 and phase 3, the initial benefit period and the re-establishment benefit period. In those two cases in 1977 the government cost was only $1 for every $3.60 paid out. In 1976 the ratio was even wider; the cost to the government was $1 for every $4.50 paid out. That illustrates that the scheme could be an insurance scheme if the government was able to keep the economy rolling, as we have been urging them to do for the many years I have been here. Because of the government's other policies which have created the situation where we have so many people unemployed and where people are unemployed for so long that benefits run out, the government has to pick up the total cost. The original good idea of having an insurance scheme to protect Canadians when they need protection has gone down the drain. The government is now complaining about the cost.
It is now the minister's intention to say that he is going to share the costs of the extended benefit period with his other partners, as he calls them, the employers and employees. I will be saying something about the plan to share that cost with other partners, but I think that employers and employees may wonder if they really need partners of that kind.
On September 1 the minister said "It is anomalous that the entire cost of this benefit..."-referring to the extended benefit-"should be borne by the Canadian taxpayer. I propose that it will now be partly financed from employer-employee premiums." Extraordinarily enough, he continues in his remarks by saying "This will in no way mean an increase in employer-employee premiums for 1979. In fact there will be a net annual saving of $50 million to $100 million to the employer-employee account. It is likely therefore that premiums can be reduced for 1979".
It is obvious that this minister learned well from his predecessor that on the one hand you can have a saving and on the other hand reduce premiums. The minister has just said by his explanation that the $2 billion deficit or short fall can be eliminated by reducing premiums. I am sure his partners will

November 9, 1978
Unemployment Insurance
be glad to read that now, Mr. Speaker, but 1 am not so sure they will think it is right or true when they get the final bill next year.
Is it any wonder, we have to ask ourselves, that the administrative side of the department is such a nightmare given this bit of history? I want to refer to a remark made by the Auditor General in his 1977 report where he had this to say about the operation of the unemployment insurance. On page 68 of his report he says:
The over-all system, when viewed as a financial system, does not contain control procedures sufficient for ensuring that claims for initial and continuing benefits are adequately validated before or after the issue of the warrant.
The second point the Auditor General makes is as follows:
There are also weaknesses in the control and balancing of data throughout the entire system that could allow unauthorized transactions to be entered or cause valid transactions to be misplaced, without being detected.
We have heard a lot over the past few years of the problems in administration of the fund, not to mention the abuses. The Auditor General commissioned the firm of Clarkson, Gordon and Company, chartered accountants, to do a study of the benefit and overpayment system of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In the report that was given to the Auditor General under date of February, 1978, we find two interesting tables showing the analysis of a statistical sample of 1,027 claims. The 1,027 samples included a total of 122 overpayments. That is a rate of 12 per cent, which resulted in the figure we heard mentioned earlier this year in the House of $95 million. I do not think that is the most important figure because the government does recover some of that. The more important figure which shows the chaos which reigns in the department in so far as the handling of cases is concerned is a different summary of the same sample results which, in addition to showing the 122 cases of overpayment, showed another 180 cases of follow-up inadequacies and 320 cases of compliance deviations.
When you add all of that, you get 622 cases or 60 per cent of claims which contained some kind of irregularity. Only 12 per cent resulted in overpayments, but 60 per cent contained some kind of irregularity. With that kind of experience, I do not know how we can expect the administration to solve the policy problems they have. They cannot even solve their administrative problems.
We will soon have the Auditor General's report for 1978. The Minister of Employment and Immigration will no doubt again be in trouble, trying to explain what his department has been doing with all its money. In his report on the 1977 accounts, with regard to the unemployment insurance account the Auditor General indicated there were $142 million in overpayments during the 1977 calendar year. That is the comparable figure to the $95 million for 1976. I do not think 1 need say any more on that. The government increases its expenditures and overpayments at about the same ratio.
I do not want the minister or hon. members to think it is just people outside of the government who think the government is

not handling things properly. I refer the minister, because he mercifully might have forgotten, to a letter which emanated from his office on June 30. I quote:
In 1977, for example, we imposed 62,104 administrative penalties and initiated 6,854 prosecutions. Over 500 employers were prosecuted. Overpayments related to unreported work and earnings and other forms of abuse and fraud were valued at $37.6 million in 1977.
Those were the department's figures, not the Auditor General's. Of course, they do not balance. If the department admits to 62,000 administrative penalties and nearly 7,000 prosecutions, that is an indication that the minister must take a very serious look at this.
A further statement was put out by the minister's office on October 26 this year. It is a five-page document explaining the $142 million in overpayments. The minister admits to 447,000 overpayments detected by the commission, a healthy increase over previous years.
The minister must also take a close look at the administrative side. I do not like to belabour this. However, there is no point in tidying up the policy if you cannot tidy up the administration. I refer to the matter recently brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt). It is raised every time there is a postal strike in this country, which has been quite a few times in the six years I have been here. I remind the minister of this because he said he would look into it.
This year across Canada there were 150,000 unemployment insurance cheques that were not picked up at special distribution centres during the postal strike. Of course, the government has explanations for this. The minister stated the staff would attempt to find out why the cheques were not picked up. He predicted the investigation would reveal in the vast majority of cases that the recipients were either unaware it was possible to pick up the cheques or were back at work and could not leave the employment they had recently obtained.
They may have been out of the country, they may have been at work, they may not have known. However, the minister was not above spending a million dollars not too long ago to warn claimants and all Canadians about cheating the system. The indication is that there were obviously a lot of people in Canada who were entitled to their insurance benefits but did not need them that particular day or week.
Perhaps it would be appropriate to try and assess the real problem in unemployment insurance. It is becoming more and more clear it is not an insurance scheme. No insurance scheme could continue to have losses as this scheme has over the many years it has been in existence.
In answer to my question in the House in April of this year, the minister said the government was considering a type of means test by which an individual's total income would be taken into account. There is something in this regard in the proposals in the bill before us. We will talk about that in a moment. In the same answer, the minister said something that caught my attention. He referred to the top echelon of the salary range who contributed a substantial amount to the fund and derived very few benefits in unemployment insurance.
November 9, 1978

The minister is sucking and blowing at the same time. On one hand he says he will tax back the benefits from high income earners. On the other hand, he says the commission are making quite a profit on the high income earners, because they pay a lot into the fund and, in his words, derive very few benefits in unemployment insurance.
The government has to decide whether it is going to have an insurance scheme or a welfare scheme, as many Canadians think it is. There are certain people in this country who are wondering about that. After the minister's statement, the Globe and Mail in an editorial of October 4 observed, and I quote:
A participant in an insurance plan is entitled to receive whatever benefits he has purchased, regardless of whether they exceed or fall short of his needs at the time he becomes eligible to receive them. Not so the participant in a welfare program, who is-or should be-entitled to receive benefits sufficient to meet his needs, neither more nor less.
On one hand the minister says there are certain people who are getting benefits who should not receive them. On the other hand, he says there are certain people who will have to pay more but they will not get any benefits. That is not a consistent view. The Globe and Mail continued in its editorial, and I quote:
For too long, Canada's unemployment insurance plan has been operated as though it were an insurance plan, plain and simple. But the plan is not funded solely through premiums, as are insurance programs; the size of benefits do not actuarially reflect the cost of purchasing them, as do insurance benefits.
It is interesting to note that in 1971 the ratio of heads of households, which is what some of the minister's amendments are aimed at, numbered about one third of the beneficiaries of the plan. By 1975 the proportion of heads of households was 14 per cent of those receiving benefits. Where is the minister taking us with these policies? Will the next step be family income? We wish he would share that information with us so that we may know where we are going. It is obvious that this is not an insurance scheme.
We on this side are calling for a complete overhaul of the system which would restore it to its original function or else change its function. We do not have the troops over here to analyze things the way the government does but it may be that the government is moving increasingly toward a guaranteed income scheme. I am sure the Prime Minister would like it- everybody gets a certain amount of the dole, enabling us to do away with all this nonsense about unemployment insurance premiums which, after all, represent merely another form of taxation. It is not a premium any more, as we know.
In past years we on this side have called for a special inquiry. Failing that we have sought a complete overhaul of the system. It was appropriate and timely for the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) just seven days before the minister made his statement on September 1 to have spoken as he did in Halifax about the developmental use of unemployment insurance funds. I think it might be a good idea to get some of that speed on the record. He said:
Unemployment Insurance
First, we will use funds from the present $4 billion unemployment insurance budget to help private employers create new jobs which give on-site training to Canadians who are now unemployed. Such a program will be of particular benefit to young Canadians who lack practical work experience but it will not be limited to them. Care will be taken in restructuring the program to ensure that support is limited to jobs which are, in fact, new and permanent. Incentives would be highest during the intitial hiring period. That program will offer employers a major incentive to create new jobs. It would give the unemployed a working wage income plus the chance to develop work skills.
Let me stop there for a moment and ask hon. members to compare that statement with the statement made by the minister on September 1. There was probably a similar desire but in no way the kind of program which would achieve what my leader has proposed.
The second proposal of the Leader of the Opposition was this:
-to redirect unemployment insurance funds to help fund the payroll costs of hiring unemployed Canadians to work on worthwhile new capital projects. I am not talking about simply another version of LIP or OFY or similar programs, too many of which fund projects of little ongoing economic value.
The kind of projects we will fund will be those which have permanent value in adding to the social or economic wealth of a community or region. The major role in deciding specific project categories will be with the provinces and local governments who know local needs better than Ottawa does.
This kind of thing would encourage Canadians to work and ease the burden on Canadians who are paying the bill. It would ease their minds, too. What they see now is money going out to encourage people to lie around instead of getting into the mood of work.
Given the climate of restraint, Canadians were looking forward to the minister's statement on September 1; people were probably quite pleased to think the government was moving to cut down the unemployment insurance deficit. The minister made six proposals. It is interesting to note they were not the same six proposals as are embodied in the bill which came out this month-we may find out the reason for this difference as the discussion proceeds. Those proposals covered a higher entrance requirement for repeaters, a higher threshold for new entrants, an increase in minimum insurable earnings, the reduction of weekly benefits, special recovery from high income claimants and the refinancing of the labour force extended phase of benefits. On the last proposition the minister said, laughably, it would be more equitable because the cost of second phase benefits would be shared.
On the same day as the minister made his statement, I made a response for this party in which I noted that in our view the measures proposed by the minister were a step in the right direction. No one would argue that it is not essential for the government to get its expenditures under control or that something should not be done, in particular, about abuses of the unemployment insurance scheme. However, I went on to say:
Even so, we realize there will be unequal hardships felt in the five eastern provinces where jobs are scarce. For example, the finding of 30 weeks of work after a 30-week claim period will be impossible in many areas. The government does not take that into account.
Toward the end of my statement I said this:
Missing from the government's announcements is an over-all plan to make Canada once again an attractive place in which to invest and to stop the flow of

At that time we demanded the recall of parliament and the presentation of a new budget. Keep in mind that this was over two months ago. We looked for an incentive budget. It did not take long for other sectors of opinion to respond. The minister's statement was made on September 1. On September 6 the Globe and Mail reacted in this way:
The federal government has finally admitted that unemployment insurance is not insurance.
The editorial went on:
Employment Minister J. S. G. Cullen has now admitted the non-insurance of Canada's unemployment insurance by tying the size of benefits to the total of the beneficiary's annual income.
That is a means test, if you like. Then the provincial governments took stock of what was going to happen to them. In addition, the churches, the missions, in Toronto were moved to worry about the effect of the number of jobless who would be on their doorsteps when people ran out of benefits and were no longer the government's responsibility. The message finally got to some of the members of parliament who come from areas which would be hardest hit by the new programs. By September 18, the Globe and Mail was reporting:
Liberal MPs from the Atlantic region are "strong and solid in their opposition" to some of the Liberal government's proposals to tighten the unemployment insurance program.
Said the Citizen in Ottawa, "Unemployment Insurance Changes are Unfair". The Journal said the new measures were a political program. The minister has not quite succeeded in that part of it, but it was interesting-

This was written by a woman. Perhaps she was angry with the minister and wanted to put that in. If I made an incorrect statement, it certainly was unintentional. I was reading only what I saw. In any event, I do not want the House to think for a minute that hon. members opposite from sensitive areas have a monopoly on compassion. There are very many members on this side of the House who are much more familiar with their areas than is the minister, and they realized the very serious implications of that bill for their own areas. My colleagues from poor provinces, if I can call them that, will be speaking in the debate and drawing these matters to the attention of the minister. Suffice it for me to say at the moment that the only reason the minister heard nothing from these MPs was that there was a summer recess. The government would not recall parliament, and even though we have been back for a month now it has taken this long to introduce this bill, which the government says is very important.
Having observed what was in the newspapers, the government decided that perhaps it was being a little too tough. The Globe and Mail was moved to observe on October 13 that the government was retreating from the stiffer standards it said it would require of applicants for unemployment insurance benefits. The government's problem was that it would not admit what the country in general knew, that unemployment insurance benefits had little of insurance about them and much of welfare. The conclusion of the Globe and Mail-which I think
November 9, 1978

will be borne out as time goes on-was that the piece by piece approach of the minister simply would not work, even if the government had the courage to stick to it.
I think it was predictable, and it is a fact now, that the bill as presented to us this week differs from the September 1 proposals. The minister did not tell us why the proposals have changed, but I could suggest a few reasons. Before doing so, I should give the House an idea of what the changes are. First, the proposal originally was that so-called repeaters would have to work the greater of the number of weeks that they had been on claim or the number of weeks ordinarily required under the variable entrance requirement for their region.
The example 1 used was that of a worker who had been unemployed and on claim for 30 weeks. He would then require 30 weeks' employment before being eligible for benefits again. The government completely ignored what we pointed out, that in many areas in Canada it is impossible to get 30 weeks of employment, and those are the very places where there are likely to be claims for 30 weeks. It is interesting to note also that the effective date of that original proposal was to be April 1, 1979. No one can tell me why it was necessary to delay the effective date seven months from the date of announcement, but now it will be effective on proclamation.
We find that the number of weeks has been changed to "up to an additional six weeks more than the variable entrance requirement." In an attempt to recognize some of the problems which I have been outlining and which the House will be hearing more about, the government then decided that in regions where the unemployment rate was above 11.5 per cent the new provisions would not apply at all. Are we to take it from that that if the unemployment rate in a particular region is only 11 per cent or 10.5 per cent, that is not a serious problem? I do not think we on this side would agree that high rates of unemployment like that are not serious.
In any event, that is one of the changes the minister proposed. Another change is that where originally 40 weeks of insured employment within two years was required for new entrants, the requirement will now be 20 weeks of insured employment or only the variable entrance requirement; in other words, the 10 to 14 weeks, if a claimant works 14 weeks the preceding year. I suppose we could say that the 40 weeks has now been reduced to 28. Again the effective date has been advanced to the date of proclamation rather than April 1 1979.
Regarding the increase in minimum insurable earnings, while the minister was unable to give any details in his September 1 statement, the provision was to be effective April 1, 1979. In the next two months prior to this bill's introduction the minister came up with details, and he now says in the bill that the minimum weekly insurable earnings will be increased to 20 hours for hourly or salaried workers and to 30 per cent of maximum insurable earnings for others. Again the effective date has been changed to January 1 instead of being April 1. That is a very serious change because there are many jobs, particularly seasonal and part-time jobs, which just do not exist for 20 hours in any given week. That means that nobody
Unemployment Insurance
who has an opportunity to take a two-day a week job, 16 hours, will be able to take that job because of the complications there will be regarding benefit rights. Instead of encouraging people to go to work for 20 hours or whatever, the minister has introduced another disincentive for people to go to work.
The reduction of the payment rate to 60 per cent from two-thirds has not changed. It has the same effective date of January 1. But the government seems to have overlooked in that reduction that for some people two-thirds of the wage is closer to a necessity, and 60 per cent to some at the other end of the scale is still more than adequate for an amount to be paid for not working. Undoubtedly my colleagues will have more to say about that aspect.
Referring to the recovery of benefits from high income claimants, the minister reduced his proposal from the $22,000 trigger level to approximately $18,000. Many workers in many cities in Canada would be faced with a problem if they lost their jobs at $18,000 or $22,000. I listened for the minister to explain how the new amounts were arrived at. The wording is 1.5 times the maximum yearly insurable earnings. If that was in effect this year, the income threshold would have been $18,000.
There has been no change in the refinancing of the labour force extended benefit stage. I commented on that earlier. It seems to be an attempt by the government to transfer the burden of the unemployment insurance deficit to the provinces. We will hear from some of my colleagues concerning the problems their provinces will have in meeting this increased burden.
Perhaps it is a good move to change the minimum fine to $200. Missing from the minister's statement was the revision of the amount of money which the proposals were going to save. In September he gave us a range of figures which would reduce the expenditures of the program because of the amendments proposed. Now he has made some substantial changes from the proposals of September 1 to the time the bill was presented; but he has not given any indication as to what the saving will be.
Another thing which the minister did not do was attack the basic problem. In the abuses and overspending of the unemployment insurance account, the basic problem is payments made to people who quit their jobs because they would rather go on unemployment insurance, or those who are fired for cause, sometimes the cause being that they simply do not want to quit and choose to wait around until they are fired. Obviously there are some problems in that area. Instead of attacking it at the administrative level, the minister took a shotgun and fired it at all repeaters. He shouid have taken a rifle to get at the 20 per cent of claimants who are estimated to be abusing the system.
Not all of those people are abusing the system on their own; some are abusing it with the help of the system. We have heard of cases where individuals, through no fault of their

own, were paid benefits only to be told later by the government that they had to pay back this amount of money. When one receives unemployment insurance, it is traditional to spend it as soon as it is received. In most cases these people have found it impossible to pay back the amounts which they have received. My colleagues will have more to say about that as well.
The minister has provided us with a further disincentive to work, especially in the seasonal job area. Apparently the government has ignored completely the fact that any insurance scheme will be subject to widespread abuse, if the replacement ratio is high enough so that there is no significant penalty to not working. Actuaries call that anti-selection or moral hazard. Private insurers have found, as the benefits increase, that the incentive to collect benefits is very much greater. Private insurers have moved to reduce the benefits paid for that very reason. It is amazing how much better one can feel if one knows he has to go to work, rather than lie at home and get paid for not working.
In addition to the government mounting an attack against working Canadians who happen to be unemployed by taking this shotgun approach rather than the rifle one, it is attacking the provinces by attempting to force them to pick up these higher bills. It will be especially hard on the poorer provinces.
I have heard that it will amount to some $80 million for the Atlantic provinces.
It reminds me of the maiden speech of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) when he told the House that we have two nations in Canada. Of course, he was not referring to geographical regions; he was talking about the haves and the haves nots. He made a very sensitive speech outlining the problems of the haves and the have nots.
The minister has created another kind of two nations: the Canadian who wants to work and cannot, and the Canadian who does not want to work if he does not have to. By its policies the government has destroyed the initiative of a whole generation of Canadians by making it easier for them to sit around on pogey rather than work.
We all know of people who accept unemployment insurance benefits because they have paid into the fund and feel entitled to such benefits. A recent study by the Fraser Institute in British Columbia indicated that no more than 10 per cent of those who exhaust their unemployment benefits go on welfare. That was more or less confirmed by Mr. St. Laurent of the minister's own department. It indicates that a large measure of the people who are receiving unemployment insurance are doing so because they feel they are entitled to it, and not because they need it. This fact is supported by the number of cheques which remained unclaimed during the recent postal strike, and only 10 per cent of those who exhaust their benefits go on welfare. I suppose this policy is an aid to the Liberal government policy of having more and more state intervention, with expenditures now at $50 billion in Canada and rising.
With difficulty this week I obtained a figure from an official of the Department of Finance which indicated that when all the government's current borrowing authorities are taken up
{Mr. Clarke.]
and after Bill C-7 is passed, the total debt of Canada will be $69 billion. That works out to just about $3,000 for each and every Canadian.
The question the government does not seem to have addressed itself to is how it is going to pay back this $69 billion. Has the government considered seriously that $6 billion, which is something like 8 per cent of the total budget, is the amount that Canada is paying in interest on the debt? When looking at the $3,000 for each and every Canadian, and that might not sound like a lot of money, we should keep in mind that the personal federal income tax statistics for 1976, just released, show that the total revenue raised by personal income tax in 1976 was less than $14 billion. We have an annual bill for interest on debt of $6 billion. In 1976 there were only 8.8 million taxpayers in Canada. If we try to relate the national debt, which is $69 billion, at $3,000 per capita, to the amount of money paid by the taxpayers, which averages out at $1,600, those who do not pay taxes are not going to help us pay back that $3,000 per capita.
If we look at the national debt on the basis of the number of taxpayers we find that this averages out at well over $7,000 per taxpayer, yet taxpayers are only paying on the average $1,600 each. We have not heard anything from the government in the six years I have been in this House about how it is going to create any kind of government surplus with which to pay back this deficit. All we get are more and more deficits. The very deficit we are talking about now in the unemployment insurance fund has been caused by the policies of this government, a government which is not considering these factors.
I am going to close, and I do not want to hear too many cheers-

There are depressed areas in the north, in the west and in the centre of Canada. Perhaps those in the east are a little more vocal, particularly the Atlantic provinces, so we think of them more often.
There are problems in the opposite direction for the working areas of the country, if I may call them that, those areas of high employment where any number of employers are having great difficulty in finding workers to fill the jobs because this government is encouraging workers to sit around rather than work. Instead of trying to get at the real problems, this government has used the scatter-gun approach.
We must stress again what can be done by this government to get the economy straightened around. This will go a long way toward solving the unemployment problem and, therefore, the unemployment insurance difficulties.

If the minister had more co-operation from his many colleagues who have held the finance portfolio during his time here, he would not be here debating this bill with us at this time. We are anxious to get this bill to the committee because we need much more information from the minister. I intend to indicate what it is that we do need. Much more study is required and many questions have to be answered. It is likely we will be proposing amendments in the committee. We want to have a very much closer look at the 11.5 per cent trigger rate for the suspension of the repeater penalty. It is entirely possible that the 11.5 per cent is too high in certain areas, and that a cut-off should be based on some lower percentage figure. The minister has not indicated how he arrived at the 11.5 per cent figure.
It is possible we will want to propose an amendment having to do with the 20 weeks of insured employment, suggesting that perhaps there should be some revision there, with some scaling on a regional basis. The minister has seen fit to have 48 regions now instead of 16 so it should be easier to make calculations and pinpoint problem areas. It may well be that in some areas a lower threshold than 20 weeks should be adopted.
It may be that areas of the bill which will deny benefits, for one reason or another, as proposed by the minister, should be reconsidered, and that certain people should be exempted from paying premiums. After all, if this is to be an insurance scheme, if one does not have coverage one should not have to pay the premium. We are going to need more information in this regard.
I have prepared a memorandum for the minister regarding information we will require. It is a little longer than I want to read into the record at this time and I will have time to do that in committee. I have two copies here which I will send to the minister right away. This memorandum requests quite a number of pieces of information about the number of unemployment insurance beneficiaries in various areas. I would ask the minister publicly now to bring the information requested in this memorandum with him to the first meeting of the committee.

During the last three years I have seen introduced in this House Bill C-69, Bill C-27 and now Bill C-14. This reminds me of the old rape victim syndrome. This bill is the epitome of placing the blame on the rape victim for the predicament in which she finds herself. 1 think in that same way we can look at Bill C-14.
Before getting into a discussion of the bill I think hon. members ought to be very clear on a few background facts. I think it is important to set the stage with these background facts. The first fact we must keep clearly in mind as we take part in this debate is that Statistics Canada tells us that on a day to day basis there are 40,000 full-time, part-time and casual jobs available in this country. I want you, Mr. Speaker, to keep that in mind as we take part in this debate.
Secondly, the unemployment rate in this country according to the latest figures is 8.2 per cent, with the number of persons unemployed, seasonally adjusted, being 910,000. The minister confirmed just the other day that in effect all the indicators show that high unemployment will continue for the rest of this year and into 1979. Those are the facts I would like to put as a backdrop to this debate in principle on Bill C-14.
Superimposed on those facts I would also like to put before the House a quote from the Economic Council.

We all know that we are debating the principle of this bill at second reading. I like to think that a principle is much the same as a theme. What is the theme of Bill C-14? I think that the theme which the government has taken is that if things can be made tough enough, if the government can dismantle enough of the unemployment insurance program, it will force the unemployed to take jobs. Throughout the government's explanation for the bill and throughout the government's propaganda we find the same song and dance over and over. The government says that it will cause more people to work because it is removing the incentives which stop people from working. I do not know how the tightening of the unemployment insurance program rules will create one single job. The unemployment rate in my own area is 11.2 per cent. How will

The government has not done it. The government made a prediction that it would create 50,000 jobs, but it created only 8,000. The program was a miserable failure, so I do not put much stock in the prediction that they ' will create jobs.
The central thrust of this bill is to make the victims pay for the predicament in which the government puts them. It is a principle which is dead wrong. We have no consideration on this side of the House where we stand with respect to the principle of this bill.
The minister announced cutbacks and changes to the UI program in September. While watching a program on national television the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, the UI critic for the official opposition, stood up, looked right into the camera and said: "If we were the government, we would have gone further with these cutbacks." Tonight, he is sitting all over the fence. He cannot do that. They will not be able to get off the horns of this particular dilemma.

The hon. member says that these people tend to get slivers, and that is right. There are not enough jobs available in this country for the number of people who are registered officially as being unemployed. I mentioned earlier in my backdrop that there are only about 40,000 full-time, part-time and casual jobs on a day to day basis in this country and that there are 910,000 people looking for work. That means there is one job for every 20 people who want to work and who are looking for work.
Hon. members must keep in mind that we are not dealing with real unemployment figures. We are not talking about the unofficial figures, which tend to be much higher than the official figures. The minister has gone into secrecy with regional figures on unemployment because they are too embarrassing, and very shortly they will probably stop producing the figures showing the ratio of the number of persons unemployed to the number of jobs available. Many of these jobs are not available permanently. The Social Planning Council of metro Toronto in their study entitled "The Problem is Jobs, not People", found that of 16,900 jobs that existed in Ontario in August, 1978 only 5,000 were available for a period of longer than four weeks. That means that of those jobs surveyed, 11,900 of them were for less than four weeks' duration. Conveniently, the department considers a permanent placement to be longer than one week with respect to collecting unemployment insurance benefits.
This legislation will not do anything about unemployment except make it more difficult to be unemployed. Once again,

the government is saying they have no responsibility for unemployment and that the unemployed are to blame. It is a lie we are becoming familiar with, a lie used to cover more government inadequacies. Legislation like this has one major purpose, and that is to cover up the fact that we have a tired and morally bankrupt government that has no policies to deal with the problems which we face in this country. At a time when it is critical for us to have economic planning to deal with a failing economy, instead we get knee-jerk policies based on gallup polls.
The Economic Council of Canada stated the situation correctly in their last annual review when it said that "in devising unemployment strategies there is a need for selective targeted policy instruments. In this way, the particular problems of women and the young, as well as of certain provinces, industries and occupations, may be recognized specifically." Obviously, Bill C-14 was conceived as a knee-jerk reaction. There was no consultation with the provinces, labour or anybody. It was conceived and dropped on the people of Canada in September of this year, and there is no doubt that the government through this bill has focussed its attenion on many of these particular groups I have mentioned. In so doing, they are trying to make a bad situation even worse.
Let us look at the situation as it applies to women in this country. I do not think the minister and his bureaucrats have spent much time looking at the facts as they relate to women as employees and as potential employees in this country. The major change this bill seeks to accomplish is to deny unemployment insurance benefits to those people who cannot find long-term work. We all know it is a fact of Canadian life today that women as a group are last hired and first fired. It seems to me they fall squarely into this category where the Unemployment Insurance Act is being amended.
Further, these changes, as they apply to women, seem to be largely based on the results of the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program that was released in 1977. That review made the dubious statement that women misuse the UIC program through non-availability and refusal to work. The review also suggested that women, as secondary wage earners, generated unexpected increases in UIC expenditures.
The Advisory Council on the Status of Women correctly pointed out that such sweeping generalizations had no facts to back them up. That did not deter the minister and his nabobs in the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They are not confused with facts and should not get credit for seeking out facts.
There are facts available about women in the labour force but the government chooses to ignore them. I will put them on the record tonight, however. Labour Canada figures for 1975 show that 31 per cent of women in the work force are single and need a job to support themselves. They show that 9.4 per cent of women in the work force are widowed, divorced or separated and must work to support themselves. They show that 20.7 per cent of women in the work force are married to

men earning less than $10,000 a year and must work to support both themselves and their families. They also show that 47 per cent of families where both husband and wife work earned less than $15,000 in 1975, below the median income.
Thus we can plainly see, Mr. Speaker, that most women in our society are like any other workers. They are working to support themselves and their families, not to buy a second car. Working women are not "a social phenomenon", as one of our Edmonton Conservatives once said in this House. They work to earn a living and as such deserve the protection of an unemployment insurance program.
This is especially true because, bad as the unemployment situation is for men, it is even worse for women. The situation will be worse yet if this legislation passes. Women often find it more difficult than men to find long-term jobs, so the requirement for people to work longer to be eligible for benefits if they have previously been on claim will hit women hard. Keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that all of this is happening at a time when there is evidence that the use of unemployment insurance by women is actually decreasing.
A comparison of unemployment insurance claimants over the last ten years in Ontario, again done by the social planning council of metro Toronto, shows a discernible downward trend in the use of the program by women. In other words, while more women need to enter the work force to make ends meet within families, they are actually able to use UIC less and less as the government attacks them, first through regulations and now through legislation.
The requirement that new entrants must work longer will hit young men and women equally hard, but it will particularly attack older women who might be returning to the work force after raising a family for a number of years. Many of these women who have spent many years in the home lack necessary skills and find it very difficult to find other than casual jobs. Many of these women go to work for such firms as temporary employment agencies. Now they will not only have to work for these leeches but they will also lose their eligibility for UIC benefits.
The same thing is true of the amendment limiting benefits to those people working more than 20 hours a week. This section of the bill is not aimed at people making a lot of money in a few hours, as the background to the bill suggests. It is aimed at the thousands of women who work part-time in department stores because they cannot find full-time work.
The federal Liberal government has talked a lot about changing the legislation to cover only those with a stable attachment to the work force, but this sort of legislation makes it clear they will never admit that women are not attached to the work force only because there are not enough jobs for them.
The author, R. H. Robinson, dealt accurately with this point in an article in the Canadian Forum. He wrote:
Working women and women wanting to work are coming more under attack with rising unemployment. There are multiplying signs of a drive, like the one which followed the Second World War, to make women believe that their true place and role is not at work but in the family and at home. Instead of being
Adjournment Debate
marginally attached to the labour force, they would be completely detached from it. This is like treating an illness, not by curing the patient, but by denying that she exists.
How familiar that sounds, Mr. Speaker, to those of us who have sat in this chamber for years hearing the government deny that the problems of this country, like unemployment, existed. The government is once again trying to have it both ways. First the government accuses women of being only secondary wage earners-those who are going to be discriminated against in this bill-taking jobs away from men. Now they are saying that they do not want women to work enough to be eligible for benefits. It is all part of the same Liberal game plan to blame the unemployed for unemployment.
I see it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, so I will call it ten o'clock.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN TO EXPORT POSITIONS
TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN TO EXPORT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question tonight arises from the continuing problems Canada is experiencing with its grain handling and transportation system. The time has come when something must be done to jar this minister and this government into action, because we have a grain handling system that is inadequate and underutilized in certain areas at certain times. It has been in this state for some period of time.
The inadequacy of our grain handling and transportation system is responsible for loss of sales in the international export market. It is responsible for our loss of reputation as a reliable supplier of grain in the export market and it is responsible for the build-up of frustration and disgust amongst producers. And to put it bluntly, it is causing farmers and this economy a loss of untold millions of dollars. Unless something positive is done very soon-perhaps even something revolutionary-Canada will suffer and lose its traditional position as a leader in grain sales throughout the world. It will no longer be in the forefront of the world grain trade picture.
We need a quantum leap in our system to capture the growing market opportunities of the 1980s. The minister has spoken of studies, of co-ordinators, of consultants and of straining the existing system. In answer to my questions on November 7, he replied, in part, as reported at page 865 of Hansard:
One of our objectives is to test those strains and to keep strain on the system.

November 9, 1978
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, it is going to take more than strain on the system to move the amount of grain we must move if we are to capture the potential market. The minister is indirectly blaming the farmers in his answer. We must bear in mind that this is the same minister who brought in Operation LIFT-that disastrous policy of paying farmers not to grow wheat.
He said as reported at page 865:
-that we have just had three all-time record crops. If only one of those had been average instead of record, it would be a problem of grain supplies rather than a problem of movement.
He is saying that it is the farmers' fault that we have a problem in moving our grain because they grow too much wheat. There is not much hope in the statements of the minister in his response to my question of November 7. Quite frankly, what we need in this country, in addition to an improved grain handling system, is a full-time Minister of Transport. We need a full-time minister in charge of the Wheat Board because this minister has been a flop in those two portfolios. I am not sure about justice; I am not qualified to comment on that, but in terms of transport, in terms of moving grain and in addressing himself to those very serious problems, he has been a flop.
We know there are inefficiencies in the system. At a recent meeting in Calgary of the Canada Grains Council the railways pointed out there was underutilization of the system, and that of course raises the question of whether we need additional hopper cars or additional rolling stock. Frankly, I think we do, but that does not mean that we should not be utilizing the system to the fullest extent.
In Canada today we have a primary elevator system that is literally plugged 75 per cent to capacity, 35 per cent more than last year. The terminals are half full, down 35 per cent from last year. The producers' stocks are up by 20 per cent; they are carrying about 42 millions tonnes of grain in stock. We are losing sales to our traditional customers. As a matter of fact representatives of the United States have served notice that they are going to pursue the Chinese market very aggressively.
Today we have a system in this country that is limited to moving 21 million tonnes of grain, and our export sales are limited by that amount. We had the promises of WEOC in 1973 and we had the promises of this government in 1974 that they were going to overhaul the grain handling system from the granary to the ship in the harbour. Since that time we have not increased the capacity one iota.
I want to quote from an address given by the senior economist to the Canadian Wheat Board, Harold F. Bjarnason, on October 18, 1978, who was talking about the 21 million tonnes that we have moved and then went on to say:
The only reason that this near record export volume did not exceed the 1972/73 level of 21.4 million tonnes was that our transportation system could not physically handle any more grain exports during the prime demand period. A yearly volume of about 21 million tonnes thus seems to be the maximum quantity our present system is capable of moving into export. If we had had greater capacity in our system, we would not have to defer 1.5 million tonnes of export grain to the 1978-79 marketing year.
[Mr. Mazankowski.)
He goes on to say:
All in all, it seems safe to say that, if transportation had been available when the demand was, exports last year could have reached 25 million tonnes.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that we have lost a sale of 4 million tonnes of grain in the last crop year and that means a direct loss to the farmers of something in excess of a half a billion dollars. If one considers the ripple effect in the economy, it works out at about $2.75 billion.
What about the future? To quote Mr. Bjarnason again, he states that:
-by 1985 we should be able to export roughly 20 million tonnes of wheat and up to 10 million tonnes of feed grains-
In addition there were 1.5 million tonnes of oilseeds. That totals 31.5 million tonnes. That means we must increase our grain handling and transportation capabilities by 50 per cent.
It is significant to know as well that the bulk of this increase will come from the west coast, so we must move very quickly. We must prepare to move well in excess of 15 million tonnes from the west coast. The most we have ever moved, and that occurred in the record year of 1972-73, was nine million tonnes. We must develop Prince Rupert and increase its capacity of moving anywhere from three million to four million tonnes, which is the equivalent of 125 million to 150 million bushels. We must expand Vancouver's capacity to reach 11 million to 12 million tonnes. That will give us 450 million to 475 million bushels. We must also move quickly to expand Thunder Bay and Churchill.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN TO EXPORT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, lamentations, jeremiads, complaints, criticism, negativism, but never constructive suggestions, never positivism. That is the typical attitude of the Progressive Conservative party which is content with destroying everything and is not-I am convinced the public realizes this-really playing the role of a responsible opposition. All the hon. member did was criticize regardless of the facts and the excellent policy of the Minister of Transport who is doing one of the best jobs ever done in the whole history of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this government is very concerned about the difficulties we have had this fall with the movement of our grain for export markets. In fact, it has been concerned about that for several years and has many programs to reduce this problem in future years.
Last year, transportation and grain handling systems moved nearly unprecedented volumes of grain in spite of the transportation problems which were much more serious than in 197273 when this record was achieved.
Capacity was increased to the point where we expected to export 23 million tonnes during the current crop year before the strike occurred which could reduce actual exports a little
November 9, 1978

under that level. This is substantial increase in capacity over the seventies when our capacity was 21 million tonnes.
To a large extent that increased capacity is the result of the guidelines the government set for the grain industry. We indicated in 1974 that we would be upgrading the grain handling system from the grain warehouses to the ships in ports. That we are doing, and everyone can see striking examples of it.
In 1973-74, the government bought 2,000 hopper cars. Since that time, we bought 6,000 more. In 1977, the hopper cars bought by the Government of Canada carried 38 per cent of the grain shipped from western Canada. Since 1974 those hoppers cars have also contributed to the improvement of the operation of our transportation system. Since then, the turn around time of cars was shortened by four days, that is 17 per cent, which allowed the average car to carry about 3.3 more loads per year.
The federal government has also contributed to the repair costs of several thousand boxcars that will increase our capacity in the short term. Recent improvements to branch lines to Churchill under the prairies branch lines renovation program have also effectively increased our grain exportation capacity through that port.
We are also increasing the capacity of grain terminals in Canada. Under the storage improvement program of the Canadian Wheat Board, the storage capacity should improve by 40 per cent in Vancouver. Half of the storage capacity increase of 5.8 million tonnes must be done before the coming winter. The rest will be completed by the end of next year.
Major improvements are being made to increase our present and future export capacity. We are now studying all possible means to transport a maximum quantity of grain through the St. Lawrence Seaway before its closing, including the extension of operating hours whenever possible. But we do not deal only with those urgent problems, Mr. Speaker, we are also concerned by problems that will be faced in the long term by our grain transportation and handling system. We commissioned an inquiry, the Hall commission on complex social and economic factors related to that system. We should soon establish in the prairies a comprehensive basic branch line system that will be operated at least until the year 2000.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF PRIME MINISTER'S COMMENT ON STATE OF CORPORATION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF PRIME MINISTER'S COMMENT ON STATE OF CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this adjournment debate on a matter which was raised in the House last week and this week. It started with a question, albeit a set-up question, from the hon.
Adjournment Debate
member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asking about coverage of the federal-provincial conference. I wish to quote the relevant words. The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi asked the Prime Minister to check with the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) so that, among other things, and I quote:
-we can determine whether the CBC is trying to fulfil or thwart its mandate as a force for unity in this country.
As part of his answer the Prime Minister said several things. Then he said:
I am sometimes amused when the CBC talks about the terrible state of the country considering the terrible state of the CBC.
That was said on Thursday, November 2. I rose in my place, Mr. Speaker. This occurred at about five minutes before three o'clock and I was trying to put a supplementary question to the Prime Minister about what he meant about the terrible state of the CBC. I know the right hon. gentleman's mood that day, at the end of the federal-provincial conference,-perhaps he was tired-but I wanted to find out whether this was a flippant or facetious remark, and I wanted him to define what he meant about the state of the CBC. After all, he is the leader of the land, a prime minister who has been in charge of cabinet and orders in councils for ten years, but unfortunately I did not catch You Honour's eye until Tuesday. When I did put the question to the Prime Minister, as recorded on page 868 of Hansard for Tuesday, the Prime Minister answered my question as to what he meant. He had the nerve, Mr. Speaker, and he smiled when he said it, to say:
-when I commented on the technical difficulties the CBC had experienced from the first day of the conference. If the hon. member had been following the proceedings, he would have seen that as a rather light reference to the difficulties the CBC had. I stand by my remarks. The CBC is very critical of many institutions in Canada. It should not be without criticism itself nor beyond the scope of criticism. I often hear it from the other side.
Those remarks were greeted with loud applause from the government benches, as was the initial statement back on Thursday. It is patently clear to anyone in this House that the Prime Minister was not referring to technical difficulties in the CBC. The question by the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi was about coverage and the seriousness of his question was for the Prime Minister to check to see if the CBC is trying to fulfil or thwart its mandate as a force for unity in this country.
I wondered if I would raise this matter in the adjournment debate or accept the Prime Minister's facetious answer to me on Tuesday. The more I thought about it the more I thought I would take the time and trouble of the House tonight to make a point that I think in capsule commentary summarizes why the mania over Trudeau in 1968 has frankly become the delirium with him in 1978.
In that remark on Thursday, without any qualification, when questions on technical difficulties of transmission were never asked, the Prime Minister replied in the most insidious form of criticism which really has been a hallmark of his administration against institutions. That, I submit to you, Mr. 998

November 9, 1978
Adjournment Debate
Speaker, is one of the reasons this country is so divided that it is searching almost for its constitutional soul, its internal soul.
I am not denying that all members and all Canadians have many strong feelings about the pros and cons, the good and the bad, the plusses and the minuses, of the only national broadcasting system that we have. But that is not the issue. The issue is not that there should not be criticism of the CBC. We all know that. But this man was asked that question as the Prime Minister of the land. Ele is not an ordinary citizen. He is supposed to be the leader of the land exercising responsible leadership. And for him to give blanket condemnation without qualification, saying "considering the terrible state of the CBC", is demoralizing to those who work within it and is most unfair.
It is not just a case of the CBC. That is a popular whipping boy. This Prime Minister, unfortunately, because he has intellect, abuses it by appealing to the baser instincts of his constituents. And frankly, Mr. Speaker, his constituents are from coast to coast because he is the Prime Minister. You can take the symbolic head of this land, the Crown, and where do we find the Prime Minister in England? Pirouetting behind the Queen. If it were an individual act, one would not think too much about it, but it was just one of many incidents which I suggest in all seriousness appeals only to the baser instincts of many Canadians.
It was the Prime Minister who not many years ago said that opposition members were nobodies. If opposition members are nobodies, let us just imagine what government backbenchers are. I do not want to proceed too far with that.
It was the Prime Minister who, on August 1, appeared on the nation's screen with his reformation after his trip to Morocco. The conversion of Saul on the road to Damascus looked like a little exercise compared with the Prime Minister's conversion regarding economic realities.
What did the Prime Minister say about another institution of ours, a popular whipping boy, the Post Office? I still remember it: "Canadians are getting sick and tired of the Post Office, and so am I". Of course he is, but the man forgets that he has been the leader of the land. He has had responsibility for doing something about the Post Office, the CBC and parliament, if he has felt so aggrieved. One of the problems of our land is this Prime Minister and his sophistry which, for those who do not know, is false argument intended to deceive. That is not acceptable any more. That is why I have taken the time to participate tonight.

Prime Minister: Then can we assume from what the Prime Minister said that he was referring only to the technical difficulties which we all noticed during the conference, that he was not making a blanket condemnation of CBC? speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

When the minister made that statement, some of us, including myself, pointed out that he was setting an objective for five years from now which would be substantially less than what was being spent by most of the other industrialized countries of the western world. I pointed out to the minister that countries such as West Germany, Japan and the United States already spent substantially more than 2 per cent of their gross national product on scientific research and development. The minister promised that five years from now we would be spending less than those other countries spend at the present time.
The truth of our contention was demonstrated this week by six background papers issued by the Department of State for Science and Technology. It reported that Canada's research and development effort has been inadequate to maintain an internationally competitive economy. It pointed out that R and D expenditures in Canada are only 0.92 per cent of the GNP Also it indicated that this ratio was disturbingly low compared with other developed countries. It went on to point out what some of the other countries were spending. The papers noted that between 50 and 65 per cent of R and D was performed by business enterprises in most industrialized countries, while in Canada, only 40 per cent of such research was carried out by business.
The minister's present proposal is that the people and the Government of Canada offer to the business corporations of this country, particularly the multinational corporations, further incentives in an attempt to persuade them to do more research and development in Canada. Despite the fact that over the years there have been a host of these programs, such as PAIT, DIP and others, none of them have succeeded in persuading the Canadian business community, particularly Canadian subsidiaries of multinational corporations which virtually do all their research and development at home bases mostly in the United States. Despite this fact and the lamentably low objective of the government, and without waiting to see if incentive programs worked, as part of its restraints program the government announced major cutbacks in government expenditures and support for research and development in the field of science.
I raised this question with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) a few weeks ago. In view of the cutbacks which were announced, I asked the minister if the government had set a new target date at which time it expected the government, universities and the corporations of this country to be spending 1.5 per cent of GNP on research and development. This percentage was announced by the minister on June 1. The Minister of Finance said that a new date had not been set and that the government was reordering its priorities.
By way of a supplementary question I asked the minister if he could explain how cuts were being made in fields in which Canada plays a leading role, especially those which gainfully employ many Canadians such as agriculture, fisheries and forestry. The minister rejected my suggestion and said that there had been no cuts for scientific research in agriculture.
Adjournment Debate
I want to put on the record what the situation is. In the Department of Agriculture there have been cutbacks in the estimates of $8.5 million for the coming year. One of the projects eliminated involved $3 million for the Lethbridge research laboratory. In the Department of the Environment there was a cutback of $11.7 million in scientific research, including $2.8 million for a Newfoundland environmental centre and a maritime forest research centre.
In the Department of Fisheries, which is increasingly important because of the 200-mile limit-and for the first time we had hopes that the tens of thousands employed in the maritime fisheries would begin to enjoy a decent standard of living- what do we find? We find a cutback in the Department of Fisheries for scientific support of $11.9 million, one example being a $2 million cutback in a technological development program which is to be reduced and eventually transferred to the private sector.
It makes no sense at all to me or to the people involved in scientific research and those who benefit from it that the government should make these cutbacks without considering the tremendously harmful effects not only on the industries concerned but the people of Canada as a whole. I would urge the government to reconsider its position and restore what already was woefully weak support for scientific research.
